title: Asking for the Whole Plan: Prompt Design Moves Language Models’ Scores on a Clinical-Safety Benchmark More Than Model Choice: An Exploratory Study on the NOHARM v2 Public Cases
content: Background: NOHARM scores a language model's management plan for a real primary-care-to-specialist consultation against specialists' ratings of the actions the case calls for. Most severe errors are omissions. The public leaderboard scores models on the bare case, with no instruction. Objective: To measure how much a structured instruction changes these scores, which part of the instruction matters, and whether the extra content is safe. Methods: On the 30 public cases (330 items), twelve models answered the bare case and five also answered with an instruction. An AI evaluator applied the benchmark's own scoring. On two models we tested the instruction's parts separately, against a plain request for 25 recommendations. Model raters and a physician reviewed the added actions the rubric does not cover. Intervals come from resampling whole cases. Results: The instruction raised severity-weighted F1 by 0.14 on average [0.09, 0.20], most for the tersest models: GPT-5.6 terra rose from 0.678 to 0.853 and Grok 4.7 from 0.354 to 0.633. The spread between models halved (standard deviation 0.17 to 0.09). Taken apart on Sonnet 5.5 and terra, the plan format alone matched the full instruction, while the request for 25 recommendations produced as many actions but scored lower (-0.040 [-0.069, -0.015] for Sonnet 5.5, -0.084 [-0.148, -0.029] for terra). Most recovered actions were follow-up and counselling. Instructed Sonnet proposed +0.13 [+0.05, +0.23] more specialist-rated harmful options per item, mostly mild or moderate; a physician reading them in context judged none harmful, and judged none of the 72 unlisted actions that a model rater had flagged as harmful to be inappropriate. One instructed call scored level with a four-call system (+0.004 [-0.035, +0.041]). The best configuration, three instructed models combined, scored 0.897 (0.869 under a second evaluator), above the benchmark's published public-case reference scores (best 0.720), though under a different evaluator and not comparable to the leaderboard. Conclusions: On this benchmark, how a model was asked changed its score more than which model was asked. Unprompted scores partly reflect how much a model writes by default, so prompted results should be reported beside unprompted ones before models, or models and clinical tools, are ranked.
